new_alt: A partially permeable membrane separates a dilute solution (more water, less solute) from a concentrated solution (less water, more solute). Water molecules pass through but sucrose molecules are too large, so there is a net movement of water from the dilute to the concentrated solution, with no energy needed. Below, plant tissue gains mass in a more dilute solution, loses mass in a more concentrated one, and does not change at the same concentration.
new_caption: In osmosis water moves from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.

new_alt: Particles are moved across a cell membrane from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated one, against the concentration gradient, using energy from respiration. Two examples: root hair cells take in mineral ions from very dilute soil water, and sugar molecules move from a lower concentration in the gut into blood with a higher concentration. Less respiration, as in waterlogged roots, means less active transport.
new_caption: Active transport moves substances against the gradient using energy from respiration.

new_alt: A cross-section of the spinal cord shows the reflex pathway from a hot stimulus. The receptor excites a sensory neurone whose cell body lies in the dorsal root swelling; it synapses with a relay neurone in the grey matter, which synapses with a motor neurone leaving by the ventral root to a muscle. Impulses also pass up the white matter to the brain. The lesson example gives a 20 ms reflex time.
new_caption: The three-neurone reflex arc: receptor, sensory, relay and motor neurones, effector, with the spinal cord roots and grey and white matter.

new_alt: Four stem plots of the first eight terms of a geometric series with first term 1. For r = 0.6 and r = minus 0.6 the terms shrink to zero (convergent). For r = 1.2 and r = minus 1.2 they grow (divergent). A number line shows convergence exactly when r is between minus 1 and 1.
new_caption: A geometric series has a sum to infinity only when |r| < 1.

new_alt: Curves 2^x, e^x, 3^x and (1/2)^x all pass through (0, 1), lie above the x-axis and have it as an asymptote. Bases above 1 give growth, with e^x between 2^x and 3^x; (1/2)^x decays and mirrors 2^x in the y-axis.
new_caption: Every aˣ passes through (0, 1); a > 1 grows and a < 1 decays.

new_alt: Blood with red cells, plasma proteins and small molecules lies on the left. Fluid crosses the endothelium with gaps, the basement membrane mesh and the podocyte slits into the capsule space. Water, glucose, urea and ions pass; cells and proteins stay. A bar diagram of example pressures (9.6 out, 2.1 and 4.5 back) gives 3.0 kPa net outward.
new_caption: Blood is forced through three layers; the basement membrane is the main filter, and cells and proteins stay in the blood.

new_alt: A graph of y = (1 - 3x)^(-1/2) with its series up to x cubed, 1 + 3x/2 + 27x^2/8 + 135x^3/16. A shaded band shows the range of validity, x between minus one third and one third. The series matches near zero but the curves separate outside the band and near the asymptote at x = 1/3.
new_caption: The series for a rational power only represents the function when |bx/a| < 1.

new_alt: Whole system of 2000 kg: 3300 − 800 = 2000a gives a = 1.25 m per second squared. Trailer alone: T − 300 = 800 × 1.25 gives T = 1300 N. With a rigid bar and braking, the system slows at 1.15 m per second squared and the bar pushes back on the trailer with 620 N thrust.
new_caption: Treat the whole system first, then one part to find the tow-bar force; a rigid bar can push (thrust).

new_alt: Six rectangles of width 0.5 under y = 2x + 1 give lower and upper totals 10.5 and 13.5. With 30 and 300 strips the bounds tighten to 11.7 to 12.3 and 11.97 to 12.03. The limit is the integral, 12.
new_caption: As strips get thinner, the rectangle sums close in on the integral.

new_alt: The graph of 5^x meets y = 40 at x = 2.29 (ln 40 divided by ln 5). Below, points 0.8^n fall; n = 13 gives 0.0550 and n = 14 gives 0.0440, the first below 0.05. Dividing by the negative ln 0.8 reverses the inequality, so n > 13.4.
new_caption: Taking logs solves aˣ = b, and a negative log reverses an inequality.

new_alt: The parabola u^2 - 5u + 6 crosses the u-axis at 2 and 3; u < 0 is shaded as impossible since e^x > 0. The curve y = e^(2x) - 5e^x + 6 crosses the x-axis at x = ln 2 and ln 3.
new_caption: Substituting u = eˣ turns e²ˣ − 5eˣ + 6 = 0 into a quadratic with roots ln 2 and ln 3.

new_alt: The area under y = 8/x³ from x = 2 to x = R is 1 − 4/R². It equals 0.75, 0.96 and 0.9996 for R = 4, 10 and 100, and tends to 1 as R grows.
new_caption: An infinitely long region can still have a finite area.

new_alt: Four cobweb diagrams with g-prime at the root 0.358 (staircase in), -0.215 (cobweb in), 2.795 (staircase out) and -1.217 (cobweb out). The iteration converges when |g-prime| < 1.
new_caption: Where the curve y = g(x) meets y = x is the root; the path converges when the curve is flatter than the line there.

new_alt: Schematic heart section viewed as if facing the person. Four chambers (atria above, ventricles below), septum between left and right, vena cava and pulmonary vein entering the atria, pulmonary artery and aorta leaving the ventricles, coronary artery over the outer wall. Further labels: atrioventricular valves, semilunar valves, thicker left ventricle wall.
new_caption: Left side of the heart is on the right of the page.

new_alt: Icons show in situ methods in the natural habitat, a wildlife reserve and a marine conservation zone, and ex situ methods outside it: a zoo, a botanic garden, a seed bank and a frozen zoo storing material in liquid nitrogen.
new_caption: In situ protects species where they live; ex situ keeps them or their genes elsewhere.

new_alt: A 90 degree sector of radius 6 cm is a quarter of the circle: arc 9.42 cm, area 28.3 cm2. A 110 degree sector of radius 8 cm is 110/360 of the circle: arc 15.36 cm, area 61.4 cm2. The same method works for any angle.
new_caption: Arc length and sector area are the same fraction, angle over 360, of the circumference and the area.

new_alt: A carrier mother XHXh and unaffected father XHY give an unaffected girl, a carrier girl, an unaffected boy and an affected boy. One child in four is affected, half the sons and no daughters. In birds, a non-barred male ZbZb crossed with a barred female ZBW gives barred sons and non-barred daughters.
new_caption: A son has one X, so one recessive allele shows; the father passes his Y to sons.

new_alt: A soft-iron core with a primary coil of 920 turns on the left taking 230 V a.c. and a secondary coil of 48 turns on the right giving 12 V. Vs = 230 x 48 / 920 = 12 V, a step-down transformer. Power in equals power out, 18 W.
new_caption: A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary, so the output voltage is lower.

new_alt: Top, a square-based pyramid with base 16 and vertical height 15 from the apex to the centre of the base. A right-angled triangle inside it uses the vertical height 15, half the base 8, and the slant height 17 on a face. Bottom, a cone with radius 6, vertical height 8 and slant height 10. Volume uses the vertical height; curved surface area uses the slant height.
new_caption: The vertical height goes in the volume formula and the slant height in the curved surface area. Pythagoras links them: 15, 8, 17 in the pyramid and 6, 8, 10 in the cone.

new_alt: Five stages show a myosin head and an actin filament with tropomyosin and troponin. At rest tropomyosin blocks the binding sites. Ca2+ binds troponin, tropomyosin moves aside and the head binds actin. The head tilts in the power stroke, pulling actin toward the M line and releasing ADP and Pi. ATP binds and the head detaches; hydrolysis of ATP resets it.
new_caption: The cross-bridge cycle: calcium, binding, power stroke, ATP detachment and reset.

new_alt: Feedback loop: chemoreceptors and pressure receptors signal the cardiac control centre in the medulla, which uses the sympathetic nerve to speed up or the vagus to slow down the SAN. Adrenaline also acts on the SAN. Bars show rest, exercise and recovery rates with blood pH.
new_caption: Heart rate is adjusted by negative feedback using opposite nerves.

new_alt: Pressure graph for left atrium, ventricle and aorta at five times (0.05, 0.12, 0.25, 0.45 and 0.60 s) in a 0.80 s cycle, with the open or closed state of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves worked out from the pressures. The cycle gives 75 beats per minute.
new_caption: Valves open and close only because of pressure differences.

new_alt: Left-hand rectangles under the increasing curve ln x sum to 1.0075 and right-hand rectangles over it sum to 1.5568, so 1.0075 < I < 1.5568; the trapezium value 1.2821 is their mean.
new_caption: For an increasing function left-hand rectangles give a lower bound and right-hand rectangles an upper bound.

new_alt: The region under y = 3/(x + 1) from x = 0 to 2 is shown with its mirror image. A thin disc of radius y and width δx has volume πy²δx, and summing gives V = π∫y² dx = 6π.
new_caption: Rotating a region makes thin discs of radius y whose volumes add to π∫y² dx.

new_alt: Making beads: enzyme and sodium alginate drip from a syringe into calcium chloride and set as beads. Using them: beads packed in a column with substrate in and product out, so the enzyme is reused and the product is pure; smaller beads have a larger surface area to volume ratio (3.0 against 1.5 per mm). Four immobilisation methods: adsorption, covalent bonding, entrapment and membrane separation.
new_caption: Immobilised enzymes stay in place, can be reused and do not contaminate the product.

new_alt: Three plant cells. Turgid: in a dilute solution water moves in, the vacuole is large and turgor pressure pushes on the cell wall so the cell is firm. Flaccid: no net water movement, the cell is limp. Plasmolysed: in a concentrated solution water moves out and the cytoplasm and membrane pull away from the wall.
new_caption: A turgid cell is firm because water pressure pushes on the wall; in a concentrated solution the cell loses water and is plasmolysed.

new_alt: A root hair cell with a long thin hair among soil particles. Labels: thin cell wall, cell sap more concentrated than the soil water, many mitochondria for active transport, nucleus. Arrows show water entering by osmosis and ions by active transport.
new_caption: Each feature of a root hair cell helps uptake of water and ions.

new_alt: Starting at 35 minutes and reading up then across gives about 77 students. Starting at 45 gives about 103, so more than 45 minutes is 120 minus 103 = 17 students, about 14%.
new_caption: From a time, go up to the curve then across; for "more than", subtract from the total.

new_alt: A tiny real cell of 0.02 mm is magnified to a 60 mm image measured on a ruler. Magnification equals image size divided by actual size, 60 mm divided by 0.02 mm, which is times 3000. Both sizes must be in the same units. 1 mm equals 1000 micrometres, so 0.02 mm is 20 micrometres.
new_caption: Magnification is image size divided by actual size, using the same units.

new_alt: Paired bars for r = 0 to 9 compare the exact binomial B(200, 0.015) with Po(3); they are almost identical. P(X ≤ 2) is 0.421 exactly and 0.423 by the Poisson. The rule is n > 50 and np < 5.
new_caption: B(200, 0.015) and Po(3) side by side, showing why Po(np) works for large n and small p.

new_alt: Bars for Po(25) with the curve N(25, 25) drawn over them. Bars from r = 31 are gold and a dashed line at 30.5 shows the continuity-corrected boundary. z = 1.1 gives 1 − Φ(1.1) = 0.136.
new_caption: Why P(X > 30) becomes P(Y > 30.5) when a Poisson is approximated by a normal.

new_alt: Two normal curves centred on 30: a wide one for a single value (sd 6) and a narrow one for the mean of 50 values (sd 0.85). The area of the narrow curve above 31 is shaded and equals 0.119.
new_caption: The mean of 50 values varies far less than one value, so P(X̄ > 31) is only 0.119.

new_alt: Cells next to the xylem use ion pumps (active transport, using ATP) to move mineral ions into the xylem. The sap then has a lower water potential, so water follows from the cortex by osmosis, building a positive pressure that pushes sap up. Evidence: sap oozing from a cut stump and guttation drops at leaf edges at night.
new_caption: Root pressure: ions pumped into the xylem draw water in by osmosis and push sap upwards.

new_alt: Two panels. In normal soil, soil water has few dissolved particles so it is more dilute than the root hair cell sap, and water enters the cell by osmosis. In salty soil or soil with too much fertiliser, soil water has many dissolved particles and is more concentrated than the cell sap, so the gradient reverses, water leaves the root hair cell and the plant wilts. Gold dots are dissolved particles.
new_caption: Water uptake and loss at a root hair cell.

new_alt: The stomach is acidic because of hydrochloric acid, which kills microbes and gives the acid pH that pepsin needs. Food then enters the duodenum, where bile neutralises the acid and makes the contents alkaline for trypsin. A sketch graph of enzyme activity against pH shows pepsin most active in acid and trypsin most active in alkali.
new_caption: Pepsin works in acid and trypsin in alkali, because bile neutralises the acid leaving the stomach.
